learning: Iteration 5 showed that a lower-inertia step (body 0.12, mass 0.6) lifted the s-bend to 13 of 20 finishes. The next race will show whether a further cut to body 0.10 helps the s-bend without raising oscillation above about 0.35.
notes: Iteration 6 package: the Builder's body_length 0.10 step on the iteration 5 design. The controller is unchanged from iteration 5, so the only variable is yaw inertia.
rationale:
Iteration 5 (score 580, the best so far) is the only validated step that broke the s-bend limit. It cut yaw inertia by shortening the body to 0.12 m and mass to 0.6 kg, and the s-bend went from 2 to 13 finishes with line losses at 0.95 and oscillation at 0.298. The slalom did not respond (0 finishes, progress 0.23, max_error at the 0.063 floor), and the oval held 20 of 20. The Builder's intent is to shorten body_length to 0.10 m with mass held at 0.6 kg, changing nothing else. Yaw inertia falls from about 0.00121 to about 0.00121 kg·m²; at these values the formula gives mass*(0.10²+0.12²)/12 = 0.6*0.0244/12 ≈ 0.00122 kg·m², which is a further modest reduction from 0.00146. I accept the geometry as proposed. The contract says body_length only enters through yaw inertia, so this is a pure inertia step.

For the controller I keep the iteration 5 gains exactly (kp 2.8, ki 0.05, kd 0.5, base_speed 1.5, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction). Changing only the geometry means any shift in the outcome can be attributed to inertia. Iteration 3 showed that narrowing the track raised the effective gain by about 11% without oscillation running away, so the gains have some headroom. The main risk is that a faster heading response adds jitter, which would show as steering_oscillation rising above about 0.35 on the oval or s-bend. The observation request covers per-track line losses, max_error, oscillation and finish rate so that case can be detected.
